chunk_findings.detail: `_cycle` must tell the victim which of *its* leases to trim, but it identifies that lease as "the first lease held by `victim.agent` whose globs overlap `asked`" instead of the specific lease that actually forms the cycle edge, which is exactly `links[vi-1].blocker` (the item the predecessor is blocked on). `_remedy` then emits `ddflow update <that lease's item> --globs <keep>` and `victim_item` is set from the same lease. Given `leases = [Held("beta","V",("src/utils/**",)), Held("alpha","V",("src/**",))]` and a predecessor `P` that waits on item `alpha` with globs `("src/utils/x.py",)`, `_contested` is truthy for both of V's leases, so `next(...)` returns `beta` (first in list order). The printed remedy becomes `ddflow update beta --globs ...` (and `victim_item == "beta"`), while P is blocked on `alpha`; dropping `beta`'s globs frees nothing P needs and the deadlock persists. The lease to release is always the one named by `links[vi-1].blocker`, which the code already has and discards.

chunk_findings.detail: The item named in the "for the others" command is the *victim's own wait target* (`victim.item` in the keep branch, `victim.blocker` in the no-hold branch), not the lease the victim holds and the others are blocked on (`links[vi-1].blocker` / `links[vi-1].item`). Take a two-cycle: `P` waits on item `alpha` held by `V`, and `V` waits on item `pdoc` held by `P`. `links = [Link(agent=P,item=alpha,...), Link(agent=V,item=pdoc,...)]`; with `V` as victim, `others == ["alpha"]` and the remedy tail prints `; alpha then \`ddflow wait --item pdoc\``. `pdoc` is the item `V` is waiting for and is held by `P` itself, so the printed instruction tells `P` to wait on an item it already holds; the correct item to re-wait on is `alpha`. This mis-naming occurs on any cycle whose members wait on different items, i.e. every real instance of the deadlock this change targets.

chunk_findings.detail:
The knob description rendered into `ddflow config` help says doctor names "the globs **the latest waiter** should drop", but the change's own design (EXTENDED 2026-10-15) specifies the victim is "the waiter with the **least progress**, then the latest claim". These select different agents. Concrete input: a 3-agent cycle where A has held long and completed most work, B has barely progressed, and C is the most recent claimant (say C just re-issued `ddflow wait --item`). The design's rule picks B and issues `ddflow update B --globs <without contested>`, but the help text tells the operator the victim is C ("the latest waiter"). Because the whole point is to name *the smallest release that breaks the cycle*, an operator following the help can be told to make the highest-progress (the latest-claiming) agent drop the contested globs, defeating the "least progress yields" intent. Either the emitted description must state the least-progress rule, or the algorithm must actually match "latest waiter"; as shipped the output and the documented rule disagree.

No other defect is demonstrable from this slice (the added JSON key is additive, both knobs are documented, and `wait_cycle`/`wait_cycle_shown` defaults are consistent between the templates and the snapshot).

Given the very deadlock in the intent (fleet-metrics holds the golden snapshot, fleet-logscmd waited longest with the least progress, fleet-logscale/another agent claimed the contested item most recently), the change’s own rule asks the least-progress waiter to yield, while the shipped text an operator reads tells them the most recent claimant is the one to release. A coordinator following the transcript’s documented behaviour would run `ddflow update <latest claimer> --globs <...>` against the wrong item, the contested lease is not released, and the cycle persists — exactly the 45-minute stall this change exists to break. The same block also names only `doctor` as the surface that shows the report, while the sibling `loops.*` knobs in this very file (`loops.max_repeated_failures`) enumerate every surface and the design has `status`/`brief` carry the yield request, so the golden text understates and misstates the remedy the feature prints.

chunk_findings.detail: The new knob is documented as "How many wait cycles `doctor` prints in full; the rest are counted. 0 prints none.", and `int_at_least(0)` explicitly permits `0`. But the truncation branch is unconditional: when `shown == 0` and there is at least one cycle, `cycles[:0]` yields nothing while `len(cycles) > 0` still appends the summary line. Concrete input: `wait_cycle = true`, `wait_cycle_shown = 0`, and two detected deadlocks — `wait_findings` returns `["2 more lease deadlock(s)"]` instead of `[]`, so `doctor` prints a deadlock line on every run for an operator who configured the count to `0` specifically to silence this output. Guard the "more" line with `shown and len(cycles) > shown` (or make the documented meaning "0 = counted only, not printed") so the code matches the knob's documented contract.

chunk_findings.detail: `own` is selected purely by "any live lease of the victim whose globs overlap `asked`", with no check that it is the lease that actually blocks the previous waiter (`links[vi - 1].blocker`). The lease to release is uniquely identified by that item, so when the victim holds more than one lease overlapping the request, `next()` returns whichever lease happens to come first in the caller-supplied `leases` list, and the remedy names the wrong item. Concrete case: victim `V` holds `Held(item="docs", holder="V", globs=("*.md",))` and `Held(item="readme", holder="V", globs=("*.md",))`; a waiter `W` waiting for `("*.md",)` is blocked by `docs` (so `links[vi-1].blocker == "docs"`). If `leases` is ordered `[readme, docs, ...]`, `own` is the `readme` lease and the report prints `ddflow update readme --globs …`, which does not release the lease `W` is blocked on, so the deadlock persists — the opposite of "the smallest release that breaks it". The same code also silently ignores the case where the victim holds *several* leases that each block the waiter; only one is ever released.

chunk_findings.detail: In the normal branch the follow-up command for the other waiters is built from `victim.item`, which is the item the victim is *waiting for*, whereas the item that the victim is about to free (and that the blocked waiter must re-claim) is `held.item` — the very item used in the same f-string for the `ddflow update`/`ddflow release` command. In a two-agent cycle A↔B (A waits on item `X` held by B, B waits on item `Y` held by A), choosing A as victim makes the report end with "…; Y then `ddflow wait --item X`", but after A drops its globs on `Y` the agent B can only proceed on `Y`; telling it to wait on `X` is a no-op command that leaves the deadlock in place. Note the sibling branch of the same function instead emits `victim.blocker`, so the two branches disagree about which item to print, which confirms the item selection here is not deliberate.

chunk_findings.detail: The change's own design note (EXTENDED 2026-10-15) defines the victim as "the waiter with the least **progress**, then the latest claim", i.e. progress is the selection rule and recency is only the tie-break. The user-facing `doc` string added here instead says doctor names "the waiter that has **waited least** (the victim)", which is a different rule: it picks by wait age, and coincides with the design only in the tie-break case. Concretely, in a three-agent cycle where A has held for 30 min and completed 90% of its work, B has waited 2 min and completed 5%, and C issued `ddflow wait --item` 1 min ago, the documented rule names C (waited least) while the specified rule names B (least progress). Whichever way the (unseen) implementation behaves, the text rendered into `ddflow config --explain` / help misstates the selection rule: if the code follows the design, the doc points the operator at the wrong agent's globs; if the code follows the doc, it does not implement the design. chunk_findings.detail: `_remedy` prints `` `ddflow wait --item {victim.blocker}` `` inside the sentence "…and {victim.agent} queues behind it". `victim.blocker` is the item *in the victim's way*, which `_edges` guarantees is held by `victim.holder` — the **next** agent around the ring, not `prev.agent`, the agent named by "behind it" — and it is not the item the victim asked for (`victim.item`, i.e. the lease the predecessor is blocked on, `links[vi-1].blocker`). For any ring of three or more agents these are three different items, so the command the operator copies does not do what the report says and does not re-register the victim's own wait. Concrete: items alpha (held by V), beta (held by W), gamma (held by P); waits P→alpha, V→beta, W→gamma; victim is V, `prev` is the P→alpha link, `own` is alpha, yet the remedy prints `ddflow wait --item beta` while claiming V queues behind P, who holds gamma. This is the earlier finding 3; the code still names `victim.blocker`, so the fix does not answer it.

chunk_findings.detail: The victim rule contradicts the change's own design ("picks a VICTIM (the waiter with the least progress, then the latest claim)"): the code ranks by wait-start time and then by lexically largest agent id. Wait-start is not progress, and the tie-break is not the latest claim — two waiters whose `since` values are equal get the lexically last id no matter who claimed last, and the agent with the least progress is selected only by coincidence (an agent that has held a lease for a long time but has barely progressed can start its wait mark later than a nearly-finished one). The module docstring and the config/golden text ("the latest waiter") match the code rather than the design, so the divergence reported as findings 4/5 is still present in the implementation, not only in the snapshot text.

chunk_findings.detail: `_edges` keeps at most one edge per (agent, holder), the oldest, so when a waiter is blocked by two leases of the same holder only one of them survives into the cycle and `_remedy` trims only that lease; the advertised "smallest release that breaks it" then does not break the deadlock. Concrete: `leases = [Held("alpha","V",("src/utils/**",)), Held("beta","V",("conf/*.yml",)), Held("docs","P",("docs/**",))]`, `waits = [Wait(item="check",agent="P",since=10.0,globs=("src/utils/help.py","conf/app.yml"),on=(("alpha","V"),("beta","V"))), Wait(item="docs",agent="V",since=20.0,globs=("docs/**",),on=(("docs","P"),))]`. P is blocked by both alpha and beta, but the P→V row keeps only the alpha link (same `since`, `beta` dropped), so with V as victim the report says `ddflow release alpha`; P is still blocked by `conf/*.yml`, nothing proceeds, and re-running doctor re-derives the same alpha edge (its `files` are now empty, degrading the remedy to "stop waiting and report to the coordinator"), so beta is never named.

chunk_findings.detail: The new probe for the remedy mis-naming fix asserts `"retries on w1" in c.remedy`, i.e. it pins the remedy to `w1`, which is the **victim's own wait target** (`V`'s `Wait.blocker`), and never asserts the item the *other* waiter is blocked on. In this fixture the other waiter is `W`, blocked on `docs` (`Held("docs","V",("*.md",))`), and per the change's own EXTENDED design the command "for the others" must name `links[vi-1].blocker` — `docs` — not the victim's pending wait. So: (a) if `retries on …` is the "for the others" line, the test bakes in exactly the wrong value described in finding 3 (`victim.blocker` = `w1` instead of `docs`) and will keep passing while the bug is present; (b) if it is instead the victim's own retry line, the test never asserts the others' `ddflow wait --item <X>` target at all, so finding 3 is still unprobed. Either way the asserted `w1` is not the lease the other waiter is blocked on, so this regression test does not answer finding 3 and the mis-named "for the others" item remains uncovered — the assertion should name `docs` (e.g. an assertion on the others' `ddflow wait --item docs` line). Given a two-cycle `W → docs(V) → w1(W)`, the correct output names `docs`, and a correct implementation that fixes finding 3 would emit `docs` here, failing this test.

chunk_findings.detail: The knob's help string, added by this change, says doctor names "the waiter that has waited least (the victim) and the globs it should drop". The design this change is meant to implement (EXTENDED 2026-10-15) selects the victim as "the waiter with the **least progress**, then the latest claim" — how long the waiter has been waiting is only the *tie-break*, never the selection rule. These pick different agents. Concrete input: a three-agent cycle `A -> B -> C -> A` where A re-issued `ddflow wait --item` a minute ago (so A has "waited least") but has already passed most of its gates and holds two of the three contested globs, while B has been blocked for 40 minutes with no gate outcome and holds the third. Per this help text the report tells A to run `ddflow update A --globs <without the contested ones>`; per the design it should name B, whose globs are the actual choke point. The remedy an operator (or `ddflow lanes advise`) is told to apply is therefore the release least likely to break the cycle, and the one that costs the most rework — the "smallest release that breaks it" guarantee the intent asks for is not what the text promises. This is the same mismatch an earlier review raised against the `loops.wait_cycle` golden text (previous finding 5, still untriaged); the wording in this revision changed from naming "the latest waiter" to naming "waited least", but "least progress" is still absent, so the finding is not answered — the text still states a selection rule that differs from the specified one.

chunk_findings.detail: The function's own contract is "0 passed, 1 failed, 2 could not run", and the failing path enforces its code explicitly (`O.Outcome(kind="ci.run", data=data, exit=O.FAIL, ...)`). The could-not-run path, however, returns `O.nothing(...)`, i.e. the no-op *success* outcome (exit 0) — the same helper used for "nothing to do", not a non-zero code. Concrete input: a repo with no CI command configured, or `ddflow ci run <item>` where `st.items[ref].branch` is falsy so the item id is handed to `CI.run` as a git ref, or any ref `CI.run` cannot resolve. `CI.run` then reports `status == "unavailable"` (the same word `_record_gate` maps to exit code 2 in the evidence via `{"passed": 0, "failed": 1}.get(res.status, 2)`), `res.ok` is false, `res.status != "failed"`, so line 118 returns an exit-0 "nothing" outcome: `ddflow ci run && ./deploy.sh` proceeds as if CI passed, even though no CI command ever ran. The evidence block for the same situation carries exit 2 while the process exit is 0, so the two disagree. (If `gate run ci`'s command is `ddflow ci run` itself — the case `IN_GATE_ENV` suppression exists for — the outer gate maps this exit 0 to a passing gate.)

chunk_findings.detail: `staged_diff` passes the file names collected by git (from `staged_paths`) straight after `--`, but `--` only terminates the revision arguments; it does **not** turn the following words into literal paths. Git still applies fnmatch-style pathspec globbing, and a path is treated as a wildcard pattern as soon as it contains `*`, `?` or `[`. Take a merge whose branch hand-resolved one file named `docs/design[1].md` (the only entry in `own`) while the merged parent also changed `docs/design1.md`. `git diff --cached -U0 -M -- 'docs/design[1].md'` matches the *class* `[1]`, i.e. it selects `docs/design1.md` and silently drops `docs/design[1].md`. The diff handed to `stale_mentions` is therefore the merged parent's changes to a file the branch never touched, so the check reports stale mentions the branch did not cause and (in `block` mode) refuses a legitimate merge commit; symmetrically, if no file matches the expansion, the diff is empty and removals the branch really made in `docs/design[1].md` are never reported. The same happens for names containing `*` or `?`, and a name starting with `:` is parsed as pathspec magic. Since the restricted diff is the whole point of the merge-scoping fix, this makes the new check silently answer for the wrong paths; the fix is to emit `:(literal)`-prefixed (or `--literal-pathspecs`) entries.

chunk_findings.detail: The item named for the non‑victim agents is the victim's own wait target (`victim.item`, or `victim.blocker` in the no‑hold branch), not the lease the victim holds that the others are blocked on (`links[vi-1].blocker` / `links[vi-1].item`). In the two‑cycle where `P` waits on `alpha` held by `V` and `V` waits on `pdoc` held by `P` (`links = [Link(agent=P,item=alpha,…), Link(agent=V,item=pdoc,…)]`), picking `V` yields `others == ["alpha"]` and the tail tells `alpha`'s waiter to re‑run `ddflow wait --item pdoc` — the item `V` is itself queued behind, not the lease `V` is about to drop. The same wrong‑item defect appears in the sibling sentence that names the agent "queues behind it". The emitted command sequence therefore does not reproduce the intended post‑yield wait.

chunk_findings.detail: `_edges` keeps at most one edge per `(agent, holder)` pair, the oldest, so when a waiter is blocked by two leases of the same holder only one survives into the graph and `_remedy` trims only that one. With `leases = [Held("alpha","V",("src/utils/**",)), Held("beta","V",("conf/*.yml",)), Held("docs","P",("docs/**",))]` and a waiter blocked on both `alpha` and `beta` (e.g. `check` needing `src/utils/help.py` and `conf/app.yml`), the advertised "smallest release that breaks it" drops one lease while the other still holds the waiter, so the suggested release does not break the deadlock.

chunk_findings.detail: The victim is ranked by `max(range(len(links)), key=lambda i: (links[i].since, links[i].agent))` — wait‑start time, then lexically largest agent id — which is neither the design's "waiter with the least progress" nor its tie‑break "latest claim". Two waiters with equal `since` are resolved by agent id regardless of who re‑issued `ddflow wait --item` last, and an agent that has held a lease long but progressed further is preferred over one that has barely progressed. chunk_findings.detail: The victim is ranked by `max(range(len(links)), key=lambda i: (links[i].since, links[i].agent))` — wait‑start time, then lexically largest agent id — which is neither the design's "waiter with the least progress" nor its tie‑break "latest claim". Concrete input: the deadlock from the intent, a three-agent ring where A has held its lease for a long time but has made the most progress, B has barely progressed, and C re-issued `ddflow wait --item` most recently. The design asks B to yield; the wording shipped here points the operator at C (the most recent waiter), and the emitted command in each case is a different `ddflow update <agent> --globs <keep>`, i.e. a different lease is trimmed and the deadlock is not necessarily broken. This is the same defect flagged before (only reworded from "the latest waiter" to "waited least"); since this diff is where the string is introduced, it is not answered by it.

chunk_findings.detail: For a ring of three or more agents the agent named by "queues behind it" is not the holder of `victim.blocker`. `_edges`/`find` guarantee `victim.blocker` is held by `victim.holder`, i.e. the *successor* around the ring (`links[vi+1].agent`), whereas the sentence attaches "behind it" to the predecessor `{prev.agent}` just introduced.
